decisions.title: Annual Plan 2026/27 adopted
decisions.outcome: Confirmed a weighted average rates increase of about 4.5% — down from the 4.9–6.5% range consulted on, and well below the 13.3% signalled in the 2024–2034 Long-Term Plan. Water and wastewater charges are now billed separately by Selwyn Water Limited, adding further to some households' bills (up to ~8.8% combined).

decisions.title: Annual Plan deliberations concluded
decisions.outcome: Following 964 submissions and near-record engagement, Council agreed to: invest more in land drainage and stormwater; approve $160,000 to support the Sheffield Pool via a community trust; cut council events funding by $107,000; and move toward more user-pays fees (e.g. an $8 increase to dog registration).

upcoming.title: Local government reform — "Head Start" pathway decision
upcoming.detail: Council must decide whether to submit a voluntary reorganisation proposal under the Government's local government reform process, or leave it to a compulsory process after the 2028 elections.

keyIssues.title: Population growth
keyIssues.text: Selwyn has experienced rapid population growth, increasing pressure on infrastructure, roads, water and community facilities.

keyIssues.title: Rates
keyIssues.text: The 2026/27 Annual Plan resulted in a 4.5% weighted-average rates increase.

keyIssues.title: Water
keyIssues.text: Water and wastewater infrastructure and the transition to direct water charging are significant issues for the district.

keyIssues.title: Roads & transport
keyIssues.text: Rapid growth is putting pressure on the road network, particularly around Rolleston and other growing communities.

keyIssues.title: Local government reform
keyIssues.text: Selwyn District Council has pursued a proposal for Selwyn to become a unitary authority, combining district and regional council functions.

mayor.name: Phil Mauger
mayor.note: Independent ("Let's Get More Stuff Done") — re-elected Mayor in October 2025 with 60,137 votes, defeating Sara Templeton (40,533). A former Christchurch businessman and former city councillor. Current priorities include controlling council debt and spending, maintaining the city's infrastructure and services, and improving Christchurch's liveability.

decisions.title: Annual Plan 2026/27 adopted
decisions.outcome: Confirmed an average household rates increase of 7.83%. Council also approved $1.37 billion in operational expenditure and $597.4 million in capital spending for 2026/27, including $15m+ towards restoring Christ Church Cathedral and other earthquake-damaged heritage buildings. A ratepayer petition subsequently called for a referendum on the rise.

decisions.title: Central city noise rules sent to consultation
decisions.outcome: The Policy and Planning Committee approved a rewrite of central-city noise rules (Plan Change 21) for public consultation, extending higher permitted noise limits in some areas after live-music venue owners warned a scaled-back map left key venues exposed to complaints.

upcoming.title: Future of the old Apollo Projects Stadium site
upcoming.detail: With the new stadium now open, Council is preparing a development plan (informed by public consultation) for the vacated temporary stadium site, including whether to repurpose, sell, or dispose of the infrastructure. An expression-of-interest and tender for decommissioning is due to be released.

keyIssues.title: Rates & council finances
keyIssues.text: The 2026/27 Annual Plan resulted in an average rates increase of 7.83%. Council also approved $1.37 billion in operational expenditure and $597.4 million in capital spending.

keyIssues.title: Water & wastewater
keyIssues.text: Christchurch is working through the Government's Local Water Done Well reforms, including the future structure and financing of water services. Stormwater and flood protection are also significant infrastructure issues.

keyIssues.title: Local government reform
keyIssues.text: Christchurch is considering major changes to Canterbury's local-government structure under the Government's Head Start pathway. Options examined include Christchurch becoming a unitary authority, combining with Selwyn and/or Waimakariri, or creating a single Canterbury-wide authority.

keyIssues.title: Heritage buildings
keyIssues.text: Council has committed significant funding towards restoring Christchurch's earthquake-damaged iconic buildings, including $15 million for Canterbury Museum, $15 million for Christ Church Cathedral, and $4 million for the Christchurch School of Music.

keyIssues.title: Infrastructure & growth
keyIssues.text: Transport, roading, three-waters infrastructure, community facilities and the ongoing development of Christchurch remain major areas of Council spending and decision-making.

mayor.name: Liz McMillan
mayor.note: Independent — elected 2025 with 5,979 votes. Previously served nine years on the Methven Community Board, was elected to Council in 2016, and served as Deputy Mayor for six years.

mp.name: James Meager
mp.note: Sitting MP for Rangitata since 2023, also National's 2026 candidate

decisions.title: Annual Plan 2026/27 adopted
decisions.outcome: Confirmed an overall average rates increase of 9.15% (5.43% for non-water Council activities, plus 13.05% for water services under the new Water Services Delivery Plan). Includes $19m for the roading network and a $16m loan for road improvements linked to the second Ashburton bridge; the FOGO organics bin rollout was delayed from September 2026 to January 2027.

decisions.title: Skipped full public consultation on the draft budget
decisions.outcome: Council decided not to run a full special-consultative process on its 8.71% proposed rates rise, judging the changes from the Long-Term Plan not significant enough to require it — a decision that drew criticism given the size of the increase.

upcoming.title: Early engagement on the Long-Term Plan 2027–37
upcoming.detail: Council will begin early consultation on its next ten-year plan later in 2026 — the main opportunity for residents to influence spending and rates direction beyond the current Annual Plan.

keyIssues.title: Second Ashburton Bridge
keyIssues.text: Construction of the Second Ashburton Bridge is underway, including piling and associated road works. The 2026/27 Council budget includes $19 million for the roading network, with a $16 million loan for road improvements linked to the second bridge.

keyIssues.title: Rates
keyIssues.text: Council's 2026/27 Annual Plan provides for an average 5.43% rates increase for non-water Council activities.

keyIssues.title: Roads
keyIssues.text: Road quality remains a significant local concern. In the latest Council residents' survey, it was identified as the district's biggest bugbear.

keyIssues.title: Local government reform
keyIssues.text: Ashburton is considering possible changes to its local-government structure. In August 2026, Council decided not to submit an outline proposal under the Government's Head Start pathway, while continuing to explore alternative reform options.

keyIssues.title: Stockwater
keyIssues.text: Council is working towards exiting the delivery of stockwater by 2027 and is reviewing the future of 17 stockwater intakes.

mp.name: Matt Doocey
mp.note: Sitting MP for Waimakariri since 2014, also National's 2026 candidate

decisions.title: Annual Plan 2026/27 adopted
decisions.outcome: Confirmed an average rates rise of 4.99% (2.9% excluding water services) — one of the lowest increases of any Canterbury council this year. Council wasn't legally required to run a full consultation but did so anyway, receiving 59 submissions; Deputy Mayor Philip Redmond called it a "responsible and prudent" plan.

upcoming.title: Government rates-capping reform takes effect
upcoming.detail: Central government's proposed rates cap (limiting increases to 2–4% per year, phased in from January 2027 to full implementation by 2029) will constrain Council's future Annual Plans and Long-Term Plan; Council has been formulating its position on the policy.

mayor.name: Nigel Bowen
mayor.note: Independent — re-elected Mayor in October 2025 with 8,424 votes, defeating Stu Piddington and Peter Bennett. Has previously served as mayor; background in hospitality, having owned and operated the Speight's Ale House and Street Food Kitchen with his wife. Stated priorities include delivering major capital projects, promoting Timaru District, navigating government reforms, and maintaining local community influence in decision-making.

mp.name: James Meager
mp.note: MP for Rangitata, the electorate covering Timaru and surrounding South Canterbury communities. Elected in 2023, retaining the seat for National.

keyIssues.title: Rates & financial pressure
keyIssues.text: Council proposed increasing the total amount of rates collected by 9% for 2026/27, citing rising costs for core services including roads and replacement pipes. Individual rate increases vary depending on the property and services received.

keyIssues.title: Water services
keyIssues.text: Timaru has been working through the Government's Local Water Done Well reforms and has been developing a water-services organisation model. Questions around ownership, costs, governance and future partnerships remain important issues.

keyIssues.title: Local government reform
keyIssues.text: Timaru and Mackenzie councils consulted residents in July 2026 about possible unitary council arrangements under the Government's Head Start programme. Options included South Canterbury-focused arrangements and potentially larger regional structures.

keyIssues.title: Roads & infrastructure
keyIssues.text: Road maintenance, water infrastructure, sewerage and transport projects remain significant council responsibilities. Current works include road renewals, sewer and watermain upgrades, and bridge and intersection projects.

keyIssues.title: Regional economic development & employment
keyIssues.text: Timaru's economy is strongly connected to agriculture, food processing, manufacturing, engineering and the Port of Timaru. Recent industrial closures, including the Smithfield meatworks closure, have made regional employment and economic resilience a significant issue.

decisions.title: 2026/27 Annual Plan rates increase
decisions.outcome: Council adopted an average 9% rates increase for 2026/27 — three percentage points lower than the 12% forecast in the Long Term Plan, after a report identified options to trim an initially estimated 13% increase.

mayor.name: Scott Aronsen
mayor.note: No party affiliation stated — elected Mayor in 2025 with 1,132 votes. Has a background in local business and community affairs in the Mackenzie District. Campaign priorities centred on maintaining local decision-making, responsible council spending, infrastructure, and supporting the district's communities and economy.

councillors.name: Rit Fisher
councillors.note: No party affiliation stated — Deputy Mayor

mp.name: Miles Anderson
mp.note: MP for Waitaki, the electorate that includes the Mackenzie District. First elected in 2023.

keyIssues.title: Rates & council spending
keyIssues.text: Mackenzie Council is under pressure to maintain essential services while controlling rates and expenditure. The draft 2026/27 Annual Plan initially indicated an 8.6% rates requirement, subject to the final plan and council decisions.

keyIssues.title: Local government reform
keyIssues.text: Mackenzie Council has decided to participate in the Government's Head Start pathway for local-government reform and work with neighbouring councils on an outline proposal. This could potentially change how local government is structured across the region.

keyIssues.title: Water services
keyIssues.text: The district is working through the Local Water Done Well reforms. Mackenzie has proposed continuing water services largely in-house while considering future shared or multi-council arrangements.

keyIssues.title: Roads & infrastructure
keyIssues.text: Maintaining the district's extensive roading network is a significant financial issue. Council has been increasing the proportion of depreciation funded for roads and using forestry-reserve dividends to help offset roading costs.

keyIssues.title: Tourism & community services
keyIssues.text: Tourism is particularly important to Mackenzie, with destinations such as Aoraki/Mount Cook and Takapō/Tekapo attracting large numbers of visitors. Council has been reviewing tourism spending and community services as part of its efforts to control costs.

2026: Council continued implementing its water-services delivery model under Local Water Done Well

mayor.name: Craig Rowley
mayor.note: Independent — re-elected in 2025 for his fifth consecutive term, receiving 1,090 votes. Has around 15 years of local-government experience. In his 2025 candidate statement, identified completing local water infrastructure, sustainable delivery of services, bottom-up decision-making, listening to residents, transparency, and maintaining strong relationships with regional and central government as priorities.

mp.name: Miles Anderson
mp.note: MP for Waitaki since 2023. Currently Chairperson of the Primary Production Committee and a member of the Regulations Review Committee.

keyIssues.title: Rates & council finances
keyIssues.text: Waimate's 2026/27 Annual Plan confirmed a 5.2% overall rates increase. Council is balancing rising infrastructure and regulatory costs with its stated aim of keeping debt low.

keyIssues.title: Water infrastructure
keyIssues.text: Water remains one of the district's major issues. Council has chosen to retain direct local control of drinking water, wastewater and stormwater, while continuing significant investment in water infrastructure.

keyIssues.title: Lower Waihao water supply
keyIssues.text: Council is investing in a new water source and water infrastructure for the Lower Waihao Rural Water Scheme, including a new watermain project and work addressing water-quality and supply concerns.

keyIssues.title: Roads & infrastructure
keyIssues.text: Maintaining the district's rural roading network is a significant financial challenge. Council's long-term plan includes funding to address a shortfall in roading expenditure while continuing essential infrastructure maintenance.

keyIssues.title: Local government reform
keyIssues.text: Government reforms are putting pressure on council finances, staffing and service delivery. Waimate has been considering how the changing local-government environment will affect the district while continuing to advocate for local decision-making.
